title: Electron-like high-temperature superconductivity induced by compressive strain in La2PrNi2O7 thin films
authors: Zhiwei Wang, Zhengjie Wang, Huiyu Wang, Mingyi Zhu, Mengzu Shi, Zongyao Huang, Houpu Li, Shoucong Ning, Jing Tao, Tao Wu, Xianhui Chen
abstract: The realization of high-temperature superconductivity in bilayer nickelates under epitaxial compressive strain is widely interpreted as mimicking the effects of high hydrostatic pressure. To test the equivalence of these mechanisms, we investigated a comprehensive strain continuum ranging from compressive (-2.14%) to tensile (+0.91%). Crucially, via ozone-assisted atomic-layer epitaxy, we realized high-temperature superconductivity in as-grown La2PrNi2O7 films on NdAlO3 substrates, which induce the most extreme compressive strain in this material system. Under extreme compression (-2.14%), these films exhibit a Tc_onset of 60 K, zero resistance at 33 K, and a diamagnetic response at 20 K, with magnetotransport measurements confirming a quasi-two-dimensional superconducting nature. Comparing our phase diagram with reported data reveals distinct lattice responses: unlike in pressurized crystals, the superconducting window in epitaxial films diverges significantly in the out-of-plane parameter c (or c/ap ratio) but remains consistent with the bulk regarding the in-plane parameter ap. Crucially, while superconductivity in both systems emerges from the suppression of spin-density waves (SDW), Hall measurements reveal a fundamental electronic dichotomy: optimal superconducting films are intrinsically electron-like (exhibiting a negative Hall coefficient), in stark contrast to the hole-like nature (positive Hall coefficient) of high-pressure bulk crystals and non-superconducting tensile films. Ultimately, both tuning strategies effectively modulate the underlying correlation landscape - the true driver of superconductivity - transcending the constraints of specific Fermi surface topologies. This work establishes a macroscopic platform for probing the multi-orbital physics of nickelates, offering a new dimension for investigating high-temperature superconductivity.
summary: This research investigates how epitaxial compressive strain can induce high-temperature superconductivity in La2PrNi2O7 thin films, mimicking the effects of high pressure. By measuring electronic properties across a range of strains, the authors demonstrate that optimal superconducting films are fundamentally electron-like, establishing a powerful platform for understanding correlation physics beyond simple structural analogies.
main_problem: To test whether high-temperature superconductivity (HTS) in nickelates is induced by compressive strain, mimicking hydrostatic pressure, or if the underlying electronic mechanism differs.
main_result: The superconducting films are intrinsically electron-like (negative Hall coefficient), contrasting with hole-like bulk crystals, suggesting that tuning the correlation landscape via strain is key to HTS.
method: Systematic epitaxial growth of La2PrNi2O7 thin films on various substrates inducing controlled strain, followed by transport and magnetic characterization.
model_or_system: The physical system is bilayer nickelate superconductors (La2PrNi2O7) grown epitaxially. The study varies the lattice mismatch to create a continuum of compressive and tensile strains, allowing comparison with bulk high-pressure data.
key_observables: Superconducting transition temperatures ($T_c$), Hall coefficient ($R_H$), normal state resistivity exponent ($n$), and superconducting critical fields ($	ext{H}_{c2}$).
important_parameters: Strain magnitude (from -2.14% to +0.91%), in-plane lattice constant ($a_p$), out-of-plane ratio ($c/a_p$).
main_assumptions: The superconducting mechanism is governed by the suppression of Spin Density Waves (SDW) and that strain tuning provides a valid, controllable analogue to hydrostatic pressure.
figures_summary: Figures detail transport ($ho$ vs $T$) showing $T_{c,	ext{onset}}$ and zero resistance; magnetic susceptibility confirming the Meissner effect; and structural data mapping lattice parameters across the strain continuum.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the platform using extreme compression on NAO substrates, systematically varies strain across multiple substrates (NAO, SLAO, LAO, LSAT), measures transport/magnetic properties, compares results to bulk high-pressure findings, and concludes by defining a structural phase diagram based on lattice parameters.
why_interesting: The work provides an experimental platform for tuning electronic correlations in strongly correlated materials using strain, which is analogous to external fields used in quantum simulation or theoretical modeling of interacting electron systems.
